paragraphs: This paper combines two components for continuous speech recognition: a multilayer perceptron that evaluates speech frames and a hidden Markov model that handles their sequence. The system works with phonemes and is speaker dependent. The neural network supplies probability estimates used by the sequence model to relate acoustic observations to its hidden states.

A central idea is to give the perceptron a sliding window of neighboring frames. This lets it interpret a sound using surrounding acoustic information rather than treating each frame independently. The authors report better frame or phoneme classification than probability estimates that lack this context, including both maximum likelihood and maximum a posteriori estimates.

Those local improvements did not automatically produce better word recognition. Several modifications were necessary before the combined system achieved acceptable performance. After these changes, a simple discrete density hidden Markov system appeared to recognize words somewhat better with neural emission estimates. The result distinguishes improving individual acoustic decisions from improving the complete recognition process.
neurips-1989-a-continuous-speech-recogni.tldr: Context-aware neural probability estimates modestly improve continuous word recognition when carefully integrated into a hidden Markov model.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to build a neural recognizer for 3,000 handwritten Kanji characters. Its construction divides the recognition task among multiple smaller networks, each trained separately on a limited set of characters. This makes the small recognizers the building blocks of the larger system rather than requiring all recognition behavior to be learned in one component.

The complete architecture has three parts. Alongside the collection of specialist networks, another network combines their outputs into a system-level recognition result. A further process facilitates that integration. This combination matters because training useful specialists is only part of the problem: their separate outputs must also support decisions across the full character collection.

The authors report that the assembled system achieves recognition performance comparable to that of its smaller constituent networks. Their finding supports the proposed construction method as a way to increase the number of recognizable characters without losing the recognition quality achieved locally. The contribution therefore concerns successful integration as well as handwritten character recognition.
neurips-1989-a-large-scale-neural-networ.tldr: A system of separately trained small networks recognizes 3,000 Kanji characters while preserving their recognition performance.

paragraphs: This paper develops a neural network to detect immunoglobulin domains in proteins from their amino acid sequences. The task includes both deciding whether such a domain is present and finding its location. The network has one hidden layer and is trained through backpropagation, making sequence-based domain recognition a learned classification problem.

The difficulty is that the relevant proteins have low overall similarity. Their useful shared characteristics are concentrated in a few conserved regions rather than spread uniformly across the sequence. A detector therefore needs to recognize localized evidence of related structure even when the rest of the protein does not closely resemble other examples.

The authors evaluate the program by scanning the NBRF NEW protein sequence database. They report very few false negatives together with a moderate number of false positives. In practical terms, the detector rarely misses the domains it is meant to find, but some flagged sequences are incorrect matches. The reported result describes a sensitive screening approach with imperfect selectivity.
neurips-1989-a-neural-network-to-detect-.tldr: A neural sequence detector finds immunoglobulin domains with very few misses but a moderate rate of false alarms.

paragraphs: This study investigates how a two-compartment neuron model converts input into firing and bursting. Its compartments contain active electrical conductances, including a dendritic potassium conductance controlled by calcium accumulation. Coupled differential equations describe the changing voltages and conductances, and the authors solve these equations numerically to examine the model's behavior.

The investigation separates two questions. To measure sensitivity to internal properties, the authors hold the input constant and vary each of the model's 17 parameters individually. To measure responses to different inputs, they fix those parameters and vary the frequency and strength of a square-wave signal delivered to the dendrite, counting firing and bursting rates.

Certain parameters governing dendritic potassium current have a stronger effect on the input-output relationship than changes in synaptic efficacy, represented by incoming current during synapse activation. Within this model, changing the neuron's own electrical properties can therefore matter more than changing input strength. The authors suggest potassium currents deserve attention as a possible mechanism of neural plasticity.
neurips-1989-a-systematic-study-of-the-i.tldr: A two-compartment neuron model responds more strongly to certain dendritic potassium parameters than to changes in synaptic efficacy.

paragraphs: This paper studies radial basis function networks whose hidden units represent receptive fields in the input space. The models combine self-organized learning with supervised learning. The authors present upper bounds for learning rates and investigate how the placement and widths of those receptive fields affect the network's ability to learn.

One change concerns receptive field widths chosen through a nearest-neighbor heuristic. The authors multiply the individual widths by an overlap factor, adjusting how much neighboring receptive fields cover the same inputs. They report improved learning performance and results indicating suitable optimal factors. This makes overlap an explicit design choice rather than simply accepting the widths produced by the original heuristic.

A second contribution is an algorithm for choosing receptive field centers using information about the desired output. It allocates more hidden units to regions according to the output relationship being learned. The reported benefit is better learning when few patterns or hidden units are available, linking representational resources to the supervised task.
neurips-1989-algorithms-for-better-repre.tldr: Adjusting receptive field overlap and using output information to place centers improves learning in radial basis function networks.

paragraphs: The paper presents an implementation of backpropagation for the Connection Machine CM-2, a massively parallel computer with a hypercube connection topology. Its contribution concerns how to execute neural network learning efficiently on that hardware. The central issue is organizing the computation and communication needed by a layered network across many processors.

The implementation mainly uses two-dimensional nearest-neighbor communication between processors. This identifies a relatively local communication operation as the main means of coordinating the parallel work. On a CM-2 with 64K processors, the authors report approximately 180 million interconnections processed per second, providing a concrete measure of the implementation's computational throughput.

The authors also argue that these techniques can extend to other algorithms for layered neural networks. Their proposed reach includes the CM-2 and other massively parallel machines with two-dimensional or higher-degree processor connections. The broader significance is a mapping strategy whose communication requirements are explicit, connecting neural computation to the structure of the machine that performs it.
neurips-1989-an-efficient-implementation.tldr: A parallel backpropagation implementation achieves about 180 million interconnections per second on a 64K-processor CM-2.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical model for analog neural networks whose numerical precision is limited. Neurons produce one of k possible outputs, using weighted threshold functions to divide the input space into regions. The motivation is evidence that analog networks can tolerate restricted precision without a substantial loss of performance.

The analysis asks how much numerical complexity is necessary for computation. It shows that weights can be replaced by bounded-size integers without increasing hardware or running time. Restricting weights further to plus or minus one remains possible, but requires additional hardware and a constant-factor increase in time. Replacing the neurons with binary units entails larger resource increases.

The paper also establishes constant-depth constructions for symmetric and general k-valued functions. A separate result shows that canonical threshold choices available for binary and ternary networks do not extend to k greater than three. Together, these findings clarify how precision, output alphabet, network size, and execution time can be traded against one another.
neurips-1989-analog-neural-networks-of-l.tldr: Theoretical results show how limited-precision neural computation can trade simpler weights and neurons for additional hardware and time.

paragraphs: This paper explains patterns that appeared in Linsker's simulations of learning in a linear neural network. Those simulations produced receptive fields with center-surround organization and sensitivity to orientation. The question is how a teacherless Hebbian rule can generate these structured responses from the statistical relationships among cell activities.

The authors analyze learning through the eigenvectors of the activity covariance matrix. A covariance matrix describes how activities vary together, while its eigenvectors identify particular patterns within those relationships. Expressing the weight dynamics in these terms connects the observed receptive fields to the input statistics that drive adaptation. The analyzed learning equation also constrains weights to remain within fixed bounds.

Analytical calculations, computational results for Linsker's covariance matrices, and general theorems explain the emergence of center-surround fields and certain oriented structures. This turns a simulation observation into an account of why particular forms can develop. The result links the organization of learned connections to the mathematical structure of correlated activity under the specified learning rule.
neurips-1989-analysis-of-linsker-s-simul.tldr: Covariance eigenvectors help explain why Hebbian learning produces center-surround and certain orientation-sensitive receptive fields.

paragraphs: The paper proposes contour maps as a general representation for recognizing two-dimensional shapes. Its starting point is their broad applicability: any image other than a blank one can give rise to such a map. It also draws on the observation that people can recognize objects and shapes from contour information.

The computational proposal is to encode the maps as long feature vectors suitable for an associative memory. This creates a connection between a visual description of shape and a representation that a recognition system can use. The contour map supplies the shape information, and its vector encoding provides a way to present that information to the memory.

The authors suggest that these properties make contour maps relevant to early visual perception. They point to the abundance of direction-sensitive neurons in mammalian visual cortex as supporting this view. The argument combines representational usefulness, human recognition ability, and biological compatibility to motivate a possible role for contours in the initial processing of visual shape.
neurips-1989-contour-map-encoding-of-sha.tldr: Contour maps offer a broadly applicable shape representation that can be encoded for recognition by associative memory.

paragraphs: The paper examines how a recurrent neural network can learn grammatical structure. A higher-order network with a single layer learns to simulate a deterministic finite-state machine and recognize regular grammars. This connects the network's changing internal state to a formal machine that processes a sequence through successive state transitions.

The authors then extend the model by attaching an external analog stack. The network can read the top of this memory and receives push and pop operations for adding and removing stored information. An enhanced neural state machine and the stack share an error term, allowing their combined behavior to be trained toward the same objective.

A gradient-descent rule derived from that error function teaches the network to use the stack operations effectively. The resulting hybrid learns simple context-free grammars and can be interpreted as a neural pushdown automaton. The key contribution is learned coordination between a neural controller and an explicit memory structure, extending grammatical capabilities beyond those demonstrated by the finite-state network alone.
neurips-1989-higher-order-recurrent-netw.tldr: A recurrent neural state machine learns simple context-free grammars when trained to control an external stack.

paragraphs: This paper reinterprets competitive learning as fitting a mixture of simple probability models to data. In the traditional competitive scheme, only the winning unit changes for a given input. The proposed view instead treats each competitor as a possible generator of that input, with Gaussian distributions offered as one example.

Maximizing the likelihood of the mixture leads to a softer update rule. Every competitor adapts, with the amount of adaptation proportional to the relative probability that it generated the observation. An input can therefore influence several units when more than one provides a plausible explanation, rather than forcing all learning through a single winner.

The author applies this approach to choosing centers for radial basis functions used in interpolation. The soft competitive model can improve performance with little extra computational cost. The result gives both a probabilistic rationale for sharing updates and a concrete application where that sharing helps, linking unsupervised organization of centers to the quality of the resulting function approximation.
neurips-1989-maximum-likelihood-competit.tldr: Probabilistic soft competition improves radial basis function center placement with little additional computation.

paragraphs: The paper examines how biological inputs can change the behavior of an existing neural circuit. Its example is the pyloric central pattern generator in the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion, a defined network of 14 neurons. Many inputs modulate this circuit, allowing it to produce multiple patterns of output from the same underlying collection of cells.

The abstract identifies three mechanisms for this reconfiguration. Modulation can determine which neurons participate, change the efficacy of their synaptic connections, or alter how individual neurons respond intrinsically. These mechanisms affect different aspects of network operation: the active membership, the influence cells exert on one another, and the response behavior of the cells themselves.

The discussion emphasizes the third mechanism, the ability to modify a neuron's intrinsic response properties. Understanding the circuit's output therefore requires considering more than which cells are connected and how strong those connections are. The paper uses this small biological network to explain how adjustable cellular behavior contributes to flexibility in the function of the whole circuit.
neurips-1989-mechanisms-for-neuromodulat.tldr: A 14-neuron biological circuit produces different outputs through changes in cell participation, synaptic efficacy, and intrinsic neuronal responses.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a parallel architecture for image compression with the goal of achieving substantial data reduction while maintaining reconstructed image quality. It frames the task as requiring two things together: a useful model of images and an efficient representation of the particular information contained in each image being compressed.

The architecture combines a Markov image model with interactions among many filter banks. The image model supplies a mathematical basis for representing image structure, while the interacting filters form part of the proposed data representation. Bringing these elements into one coherent architecture is the paper's approach to connecting assumptions about images with the machinery used to encode them.

The design draws inspiration from physiological knowledge of multiple channels in human vision and the interactions between those channels. Its emphasis is therefore on coordinated processing across filters, with parallel organization built into the proposal. The contribution described is an architecture aimed at balancing compression and reconstruction quality through an image model and interacting representations.
neurips-1989-model-based-image-compressi.tldr: A proposed image-compression architecture combines a Markov image model with parallel, interacting filter banks inspired by human vision.

paragraphs: This paper explores how a neural network can produce behavior shaped by an internal motivational state. Its starting point is that an animal's response to its surroundings depends partly on internal drives. Understanding behavior therefore involves explaining how those drives influence the relationship between environmental information and the actions an animal performs.

The authors build a heterogeneous artificial neural network to control feeding in a simulated insect. Their design draws on research into the neural basis of feeding in the marine mollusc Aplysia. This uses a biological account of one feeding system to guide the construction of an artificial controller whose behavior can be observed in simulation.

The simulated insect's feeding shares many characteristics with motivated behavior in natural animals, according to the authors. The significance is that the network provides a working computational example of the connection between neural control and motivation. Feeding serves as the concrete behavior through which the study examines how internally governed responses can emerge in an artificial animal.
neurips-1989-neural-implementation-of-mo.tldr: A biologically inspired neural controller gives a simulated insect feeding behavior resembling motivation in natural animals.

paragraphs: The paper studies networks in which neurons emit spikes according to a Poisson process. Each cell's state is described by its instantaneous firing rate. At high firing rates, the model approaches the Hopfield model, establishing a connection between the spiking formulation and a familiar description based on continuously represented neural activity.

Explicit spikes introduce effects that change the network's dynamics. Spike-related noise produces an asymmetry between cells' on and off states. The model also develops probability currents, which invalidate the usual account of network behavior in terms of an energy surface. Spiking therefore changes the structure of the dynamics rather than merely adding fluctuations to an otherwise equivalent model.

The formulation also connects network parameters, including synaptic weights, to experimental measurements of real synapses. Incorporating realistic postsynaptic responses further alters the dynamics and suggests a possible dynamical learning mechanism. The paper thus ties the mathematical consequences of spikes to the physical response properties of synapses and their potential role in learning.
neurips-1989-non-boltzmann-dynamics-in-n.tldr: Explicit spiking creates asymmetries and probability currents that undermine the usual energy-surface description of neural network dynamics.

paragraphs: This paper asks how modular connection patterns can develop in a neural network that initially has no preferred spatial locations. It takes biological structures such as cortical columns and olfactory glomeruli as motivation. The proposed explanation begins with localized patterns of collective activity in a layer of interacting cells.

These activity patterns shape anatomical connections through Hebbian learning. Although the network starts spatially homogeneous, localized collective excitations emerge spontaneously and are followed by modular connectivity. The authors describe this as breaking translational symmetry: locations that were initially equivalent acquire different roles as organized spatial structure develops. They relate the process to pattern formation in reaction-diffusion systems.

The analysis identifies requirements involving lateral connection patterns and the gains of individual units that are essential for modularity to develop. Thus, the explanation depends on specific properties of network interaction and responsiveness. The authors expect these requirements to remain relevant in more biologically realistic models, presenting the simple system as a way to isolate conditions underlying modular organization.
neurips-1989-note-on-development-of-modu.tldr: Localized collective activity can organize an initially uniform neural network into modules through Hebbian learning.

paragraphs: The paper compares multilayer perceptrons with trained classification trees. Both can represent arbitrary nonlinear classifications when enough data and time are available, but they organize their decisions differently. The authors first examine those differences and conclude that theory does not provide a sufficient basis for declaring either method clearly superior.

They therefore compare the methods empirically on three applications: power system load forecasting, power system security prediction, and vowel identification across speakers. These tasks provide concrete settings in which to assess the alternatives. The comparison includes piecewise-linear trees, so the tree side is not restricted to its simplest possible decision structure.

Across the reported tests, the multilayer perceptron performs at least as well as the trained classification trees and sometimes better. This supplies evidence favoring the perceptron for the applications examined, while the authors' initial argument explains why practical testing was necessary. The contribution is a consistent empirical comparison across several problems in the absence of a clear theoretical ranking.
neurips-1989-performance-comparisons-bet.tldr: Multilayer perceptrons match or outperform trained classification trees across three tested real-world applications.

paragraphs: This study compares eight neural and conventional classifiers on two speech recognition tasks and two artificial tasks. The implementations run on a serial computer. The set includes Gaussian classification, nearest neighbors, two backpropagation variants, hypersphere and feature-map methods, learning vector quantization, and a binary decision tree.

Error rates are statistically equivalent on almost all tasks, but the systems differ by orders of magnitude in practical resource requirements. The comparison considers memory, training time, classification time, and ease of adaptation. Nearest-neighbor methods train quickly but use the most memory. Trees classify quickly but are complicated to adapt, while backpropagation usually requires long training and intermediate memory.

The findings shift attention toward the conditions under which a classifier will operate. When error rates are similar, available storage, allowable preparation time, response speed, and adaptation needs become consequential selection criteria. The paper's main lesson is that evaluating recognition quality alone can miss large differences in the cost and practicality of obtaining that quality.
neurips-1989-practical-characteristics-o.tldr: Eight classifiers achieve mostly similar error rates but differ dramatically in memory, speed, and adaptability.

paragraphs: This paper develops analog integrated circuits for early and intermediate visual processing. The approach uses resistive networks as the basis for implementing vision algorithms in hardware. The laboratory's broader goal is to turn these circuit structures into working components for computer vision and robotics that operate in real time.

Two circuits illustrate the approach. An experimental resistive-fuse circuit smooths and segments depth data that are noisy and sparse. Another performs one-dimensional edge detection by computing zero crossings using two resistive grids with different spatial constants. The examples address both organizing imperfect depth information and detecting changes in a visual signal through analog circuit operations.

The authors have fabricated analog CMOS VLSI chips and describe mounting the circuits on small mobile vehicles in a laboratory environment. This integration is intended to demonstrate the robustness of the algorithms and their hardware implementations during real-time operation. The contribution brings together visual processing methods, physical circuit realizations, and a robotic setting in which those components can be exercised.
neurips-1989-real-time-computer-vision-a.tldr: Analog resistive-network circuits implement depth processing and edge detection for integration into small real-time robotic vehicles.

paragraphs: This paper trains multilayer neural networks to recognize handwritten digits scanned from bank checks and letters entered with a stylus digitizer. With a large training set and enough network capacity to fit it well, typical error rates are 4–5% when every input receives a decision and 1–2% when 10% are rejected.

The authors find that network topology and capacity, measured by connection count, have surprisingly little influence on generalization under these conditions. They argue that a large, representative training sample may be the most important ingredient for practical recognition accuracy. Scientifically, this challenges the relevance of learning models that predict backpropagation's generalization mainly from estimates of network capacity.

Reducing capacity nevertheless has other benefits, particularly when achieved through local receptive fields and shared weights. Networks built this way develop feature detectors resembling those found in visual cortex and orientation-selective units described by Linsker. The results distinguish the importance of training coverage for recognition performance from the representational effects of particular architectural constraints.
neurips-1989-recognizing-hand-printed-le.tldr: Large, representative training sets matter more than connection count for the reported handwritten character recognition performance.

paragraphs: CHIR, or Learning by Choice of Internal Representations, approaches training by treating a network's internal representations as the main objects to determine. Many learning methods search directly for weights that minimize a cost. CHIR instead searches over the internal activity representations that the network should use to carry out its task.

Weight adaptation cooperates with this representation search, using a method such as the perceptron learning rule. The paper presents a generalized form of CHIR that extends the original single-output version to feedforward networks of binary neurons. This broadens the architecture to which the representation-centered training procedure can be applied.

The authors further modify CHIR for networks whose weights are restricted to plus or minus one. Binary neuron outputs and binary connection weights are separate restrictions, and this extension addresses the latter explicitly. Preliminary tests on the random teacher problem illustrate the binary-weight version. The contribution is the algorithm's adaptability across these network constraints, with the reported evaluation characterized as preliminary.
neurips-1989-the-chir-algorithm-for-feed.tldr: CHIR trains through a search over internal representations and is extended to feedforward networks with binary weights.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a Self Organizing Neural Network algorithm, SONN, for separating a mixture of two signals. The specific task combines male speech with a modem data signal, transmits the sum through a 4 kHz channel, and samples it at 8 kHz. Supervised learning is used in an attempt to reconstruct the original signals.

The comparison is with a network trained by backpropagation. SONN's distinctive feature is that it constructs its network topology during training. Architecture selection therefore becomes part of the learning procedure, addressing the trial-and-error process associated with designing the backpropagation network used for comparison.

The authors report that SONN produces a much smaller network and trains faster. These findings concern the resources and design effort needed for the separation application. The contribution is a supervised approach that adapts its structure while learning, demonstrated on a mixture of speech and data. The reported advantages connect automatic topology construction to network compactness and training efficiency in that setting.
neurips-1989-the-cocktail-party-problem-.tldr: SONN builds its own topology and yields a smaller, faster-training network for supervised speech-and-data signal separation.

paragraphs: The paper derives a method for training how a neural network behaves over time. It applies to discrete-time networks with arbitrary feedback, allowing the training problem to involve recurrent interactions rather than only a one-way passage from input to output. The objective is to learn dynamical behavior through a gradient-based optimization procedure.

Like backpropagation, the method minimizes an error function. Its distinctive choice is where optimization occurs: the hidden portion of the network's state space can be adjusted instead of, or alongside, its weights. This makes internal states part of the training search, expanding the quantities through which the desired behavior can be pursued.

The authors present computational results on simple dynamical tasks. One requires responding to a signal encountered 100 time steps earlier, making delayed influence a concrete part of the evaluation. The paper's contribution is a training formulation centered on hidden states, together with examples that exercise temporal behavior and a dependency extending far back in the input sequence.
neurips-1989-the-moving-targets-training.tldr: Moving Targets trains network dynamics by optimizing hidden states, alone or alongside weights, including on a task with a 100-step delay.

paragraphs: TRAFFIC is a model for recognizing two-dimensional shapes in images that have not already been divided into separate objects. Recognition is designed to work regardless of an object's position, orientation, or scale. The approach focuses on the structural relationship between an object and the features that make it up.

Each feature has a reference frame, and the network's weights encode a fixed transformation from that frame to the object's frame. This represents how a component relates to the whole in a way that remains consistent across the stated viewpoint changes. A hierarchy combines these transformations, with successive layers representing increasingly complex features.

The hierarchical construction allows the network to recognize multiple objects in parallel. The paper describes an implementation and experiments recognizing constellations of stars despite changes in viewpoint. These results demonstrate the proposed use of component-to-object transformations in a concrete recognition setting. The central idea is that encoding stable structural relationships can support recognition even when the image coordinates of the object change.
neurips-1989-traffic-recognizing-objects.tldr: TRAFFIC recognizes shapes across position, rotation, and scale changes by combining hierarchical transformations between feature and object reference frames.

paragraphs: This paper discusses using a neural network to classify electrocardiogram signals directly. Normal heart activity and dangerous arrhythmias produce distinctive signal patterns. Some monitoring devices first turn the waveform into a set of parameters and diagnose from those values; the proposed approach instead makes the ECG signal itself the basis for neural classification.

A central requirement is translation invariance. When an ECG segment is selected arbitrarily, a diagnostic feature can occur at different positions within that segment. Its location should therefore not determine how the network interprets it. The input representation must preserve useful pattern information while allowing the same feature to be recognized wherever it appears.

The author also identifies variation across patients and across separate episodes as something the input must tolerate. Together, these requirements define the representation problem behind direct ECG classification: retain the distinctions relevant to rhythm diagnosis while reducing sensitivity to timing position and other rhythm variability. The contribution described is an approach organized around those necessary properties of the network's input.
neurips-1989-using-a-translation-invaria.tldr: Direct neural ECG classification requires inputs that tolerate shifts in feature position and variation across patients and episodes.
